display_name: Plantagenet Omrah Pinot Noir, Great Southern
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "A cool-climate Great Southern Pinot Noir from the 2011 vintage that carries the region's maritime acidity and mineral bite from granite- and gneiss-derived soils. The bronze medal at TEXSOM signals a solid regional example rather than a show-stopping trophy wine.",
  "wine_summary": "This Omrah Pinot Noir is a snapshot of Great Southern's cooler, southern maritime belt: restrained red-fruit aromas, mid-weight palate, and a chalky mineral thread. Plantagenet is a long-standing Western Australia producer whose regional bottlings typically aim to reflect site clarity over heavy extraction; here that intent translates into a Pinot that trades overt oak for fresh acidity and savory detail. The 2011 vintage in Great Southern offered cooler ripening and preservation of natural acidity, which underpins the wine's structure and keeps flavors focused on cherry, cranberry and iron-like minerality.",
  "terroir_expression": "Great Southern soils — notably granite and gneissic sandy loams along with lateritic gravelly sandy loams and marri/karri loams — deliver free-draining profiles and modest vine vigor; that stress concentrates red-fruit flavours and produces higher skin-to-juice ratios, giving the wine its bright red cherry notes and a stony, almost iron-tinged mineral streak. The region's strong maritime influence (cool afternoon breezes from the Southern Ocean) extends hang-time, retaining acidity and producing Pinot with lifted aromatics and relatively soft tannins.",
  "vinification_summary": "Specific vinification details for the 2011 Omrah release are not publicly documented; regional practice for Great Southern Pinot at that time favored cool ferment temperatures to preserve volatile aromatics, moderate extraction to avoid aggressive tannin, and maturation in primarily older French oak with limited new oak to avoid overpowering the fruit. Note: malolactic fermentation (the conversion of sharper malic acid to softer lactic acid) is commonly used to round Pinot Noir's acidity in this climate and would explain the wine's smooth mid-palate if it occurred.",
  "food_pairing": "Casual — Nashville hot chicken with a cooling slaw: the wine's acidity cuts the heat and bright red-fruit complements the spicy glaze.\nCasual — Wood-fired pizza with prosciutto and wild mushrooms: the savory mushroom note echoes the wine's earthy, granite-influenced character while the acid refreshes the palate.\nFine dining — Seared duck breast with cherry-port jus and roasted beetroot: matching the wine's red-fruit and supporting its acidity keeps the dish lively without overpowering the bird.\nFine dining — Wild mushroom risotto finished with aged Parmigiano-Reggiano: the wine's moderate tannin and mineral thread pairs with the umami and cream of the risotto.\nCasual/Seafood — Tasmanian salmon with preserved lemon and capers: acidity and red-fruit lift the oiliness of the fish while the capers harmonize with the wine's savory edge.",
  "comparable_wines": "Howard Park 'Scotsdale' Pinot Noir — why it's comparable: another Great Southern Pinot that balances cool-climate acidity with granite-influenced minerality and moderate oak usage.\nSinglefile Pinot Noir (Porongurup) — why it's comparable: sourced from a nearby subregion with similar elevated sites and granite soils producing bright, savory Pinot Noir.",
  "style_profile": "Medium-bodied dry Pinot Noir with bright acidity and savory, granite-driven minerality",
  "cellar_recommendation": "If you have bottles now, drink them within the next 1–3 years; remaining freshness will rely on cool, steady storage (12–14°C, moderate humidity) and avoiding heat fluctuations.",
  "value_assessment": "AUD 20–30: At this price the Omrah Pinot sits alongside entry-to-mid-level Great Southern Pinots (e.g., Howard Park single-vineyard offerings) and represents reasonable value for a cool-climate regional Pinot. Buy it if you want a food-friendly, tertiary-stage Pinot with savory complexity rather than a musclebound new-world fruit bomb.",
  "market_position": "This wine fits on regional restaurant lists and retail shelves aimed at diners seeking an Australian Pinot with Old-World restraint rather than collectors chasing investment-grade bottles. It appeals to sommeliers building coastal or Australian regional lists and to consumers who prefer Pinot Noir that pairs easily with a range of dishes.",

If you want a Pinot for immediate pairing with mushroom or poultry dishes, buy; if you want big, ageworthy fruit, look toward higher-priced single-vineyard bottlings from Mount Barker or Porongurup.",

parsed.hook: A cool-climate Great Southern Pinot Noir from the 2011 vintage that carries the region's maritime acidity and mineral bite from granite- and gneiss-derived soils. The bronze medal at TEXSOM signals a solid regional example rather than a show-stopping trophy wine.
parsed.wine_summary: This Omrah Pinot Noir is a snapshot of Great Southern's cooler, southern maritime belt: restrained red-fruit aromas, mid-weight palate, and a chalky mineral thread. Plantagenet is a long-standing Western Australia producer whose regional bottlings typically aim to reflect site clarity over heavy extraction; here that intent translates into a Pinot that trades overt oak for fresh acidity and savory detail. The 2011 vintage in Great Southern offered cooler ripening and preservation of natural acidity, which underpins the wine's structure and keeps flavors focused on cherry, cranberry and iron-like minerality.
parsed.terroir_expression: Great Southern soils — notably granite and gneissic sandy loams along with lateritic gravelly sandy loams and marri/karri loams — deliver free-draining profiles and modest vine vigor; that stress concentrates red-fruit flavours and produces higher skin-to-juice ratios, giving the wine its bright red cherry notes and a stony, almost iron-tinged mineral streak. The region's strong maritime influence (cool afternoon breezes from the Southern Ocean) extends hang-time, retaining acidity and producing Pinot with lifted aromatics and relatively soft tannins.
parsed.vinification_summary: Specific vinification details for the 2011 Omrah release are not publicly documented; regional practice for Great Southern Pinot at that time favored cool ferment temperatures to preserve volatile aromatics, moderate extraction to avoid aggressive tannin, and maturation in primarily older French oak with limited new oak to avoid overpowering the fruit. Note: malolactic fermentation (the conversion of sharper malic acid to softer lactic acid) is commonly used to round Pinot Noir's acidity in this climate and would explain the wine's smooth mid-palate if it occurred.
parsed.food_pairing:
Casual — Nashville hot chicken with a cooling slaw: the wine's acidity cuts the heat and bright red-fruit complements the spicy glaze.
Casual — Wood-fired pizza with prosciutto and wild mushrooms: the savory mushroom note echoes the wine's earthy, granite-influenced character while the acid refreshes the palate.
Fine dining — Seared duck breast with cherry-port jus and roasted beetroot: matching the wine's red-fruit and supporting its acidity keeps the dish lively without overpowering the bird.
Fine dining — Wild mushroom risotto finished with aged Parmigiano-Reggiano: the wine's moderate tannin and mineral thread pairs with the umami and cream of the risotto.
Casual/Seafood — Tasmanian salmon with preserved lemon and capers: acidity and red-fruit lift the oiliness of the fish while the capers harmonize with the wine's savory edge.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Howard Park 'Scotsdale' Pinot Noir — why it's comparable: another Great Southern Pinot that balances cool-climate acidity with granite-influenced minerality and moderate oak usage.
Singlefile Pinot Noir (Porongurup) — why it's comparable: sourced from a nearby subregion with similar elevated sites and granite soils producing bright, savory Pinot Noir.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-bodied dry Pinot Noir with bright acidity and savory, granite-driven minerality
parsed.cellar_recommendation: If you have bottles now, drink them within the next 1–3 years; remaining freshness will rely on cool, steady storage (12–14°C, moderate humidity) and avoiding heat fluctuations.
parsed.value_assessment: AUD 20–30: At this price the Omrah Pinot sits alongside entry-to-mid-level Great Southern Pinots (e.g., Howard Park single-vineyard offerings) and represents reasonable value for a cool-climate regional Pinot. Buy it if you want a food-friendly, tertiary-stage Pinot with savory complexity rather than a musclebound new-world fruit bomb.
parsed.market_position: This wine fits on regional restaurant lists and retail shelves aimed at diners seeking an Australian Pinot with Old-World restraint rather than collectors chasing investment-grade bottles. It appeals to sommeliers building coastal or Australian regional lists and to consumers who prefer Pinot Noir that pairs easily with a range of dishes.
parsed.insider_take: Treat this as a drinking bottle, not a cellar bet: the tradeoff is clarity and savory detail at the expense of long-term structure. If you want a Pinot for immediate pairing with mushroom or poultry dishes, buy; if you want big, ageworthy fruit, look toward higher-priced single-vineyard bottlings from Mount Barker or Porongurup.
